final_text:
## Incident Report — 2024-07-30 Traffic Analysis Exercise

**Evidence reviewed:** `2024-07-30-traffic-analysis-exercise.pcap` (11,562 frames, 585.7 sec, 2024-07-30 06:38:48–06:48:34 UTC+4). No IDS/Suricata alert exports or other artifacts were present in the evidence directory — attribution is based entirely on packet content.

### Victim host
- **IPv4:** 172.16.1.66
- **MAC:** 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08 (Intel Corporate), confirmed bound to .66 via ARP (frames 9066/9068, 11550/11552) and consistent across the whole capture
- **Windows hostname:** DESKTOP-SKBR25F (seen in DNS queries, NBNS name registration, and Kerberos)
- **Logged-in user:** `ccollier` (confirmed twice: Kerberos `CNameString` from 172.16.1.66, and independently self-reported inside the malware's own C2 beacon)
- **Domain/DC:** wiresharkworkshop.online, DC = WIRESHARK-WS-DC (172.16.1.4, MAC 5c:f9:dd:8c:97:35) — this is the normal AD environment, not an indicator of compromise

### Malware family
**STRRAT** (Java-based RAT/info-stealer), version **1.6**. **Signature-confirmed** — not behavioral inference. The malware's own C2 beacon literally self-identifies:

```
ping|STRRAT|1BE8292C|DESKTOP-SKBR25F|ccollier|Microsoft Windows 11 Pro|64-bit|Windows Defender|UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy|1.6|US:United States|Not Installed|4 min 40 sec
```

(the base64 field `UHJvZ3JhbSBNYW5hZ2Vy` decodes to `Program Manager`, the active window title — consistent with STRRAT's known active-window-tracking beacon field). This pipe-delimited "ping|STRRAT|\<botID\>|\<hostname\>|\<user\>|\<OS\>|..." format is STRRAT's documented C2 protocol.

### Command-and-control activity
A single persistent raw-TCP session (tcp.stream 83) opened at 2024-07-30T06:40:05+04:00 (frame 9066) and continued for the remainder of the capture (through frame 11562, ~585 sec). No TLS, no HTTP — plaintext pipe-delimited beacon over a non-standard port. The client sends a 3-digit ASCII length prefix (`"136\r\n\r\n"`, `"137\r\n\r\n"`, etc.) followed by the ping payload, roughly every 5 seconds; the counter field ("1 Sec" → "4 min 40 sec" → ...) confirms an incrementing beacon interval, not a replay/artifact. 102 full ping messages were observed.

No DNS query in the capture resolves to the C2 IP — the malware connects to a hardcoded IP:port with no domain lookup.

### Grounded IOCs

| Type | Value | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| C2 endpoint | **141.98.10.79:12132** | tcp.stream 83, frames 9066–11562; raw TCP, no TLS/HTTP, sole non-standard-port destination in capture |
| Malware self-ID string | `STRRAT` / bot ID `1BE8292C` / version `1.6` | plaintext in every beacon payload, e.g. frame 9119, 11525 |

No malicious domain, malicious URL, transferred file, or file hash could be grounded in this capture. `tshark --export-objects http` recovered only two benign objects (`connecttest.txt` — Microsoft NCSI check, and a JSON response from `ip-api.com`, a legitimate geolocation lookup also commonly abused by malware for victim geo-fingerprinting but not itself malicious). All other traffic is TLS-encrypted with no available decryption keys, so no payload, delivery URL, or dropped-file artifact is visible. The capture appears to begin after initial infection — the delivery/dropper stage (typically a malspam JAR/PDF lure for STRRAT) is not present in this pcap.

### Benign context (not IOCs)
Microsoft/Office 365 telemetry and auth (login.microsoftonline.com, *.office.com, *.msn.com, events.data.microsoft.com, etc.), Bing/Skype/Windows services, github.com/objects.githubusercontent.com, repo1.maven.org, javadl-esd-secure.oracle.com (Java auto-update), AD/DC traffic to 172.16.1.4 (LDAP, Kerberos, SMB2, DCE/RPC), and `ip-api.com` (single benign-looking geolocation lookup, though notable as a technique also used by malware for victim fingerprinting).

### Summary
The Windows 11 workstation **DESKTOP-SKBR25F** (172.16.1.66, MAC 00:1e:64:ec:f3:08), logged in as user **ccollier**, is infected with the **STRRAT v1.6** Java RAT (signature-confirmed via self-identifying C2 beacon strings). Roughly 90 seconds after capture start the host opened a persistent raw-TCP beacon to **141.98.10.79:12132** and maintained it for the entire ~10-minute capture, sending host/user/OS fingerprint and active-window data every ~5 seconds. The infection vector (delivery/dropper) is not present in this capture; no malicious file or hash could be recovered.
